Cyclic Incenters

GeometryCirclesTriangles
Game: This is a picture, not a game: four dots on a round loop make a box around it, and four small circles inside always sit on another round loop.
How to play: Drag the dots A, B, C and D, or focus a dot and use the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to show circles, lines and names.
Look for the math

Move one dot and the whole drawing changes, yet four small circle centres keep landing on one circle. This is Christopher Bradley's conjecture, proved by Darij Grinberg on the cut-the-knot page. The live article still embeds the Java applet it describes; here the four dots of that applet are draggable with a mouse or the arrow keys.

A box around the circle

The four dots lie on one circle. At each dot the applet draws the tangent to that circle; neighbouring tangents meet in a four-sided figure with the circle as its incircle. Such a figure is a tangential quadrilateral: its opposite sides add up the same way, AB + CD = BC + DA. The logic test checks that all four sides stay one radius from the centre, to drawing precision.

Four triangles around the crossing

Where the box's diagonals cross, call the point P. The triangles PAB, PBC, PCD and PDA each have an incenter, marked X, Y, Z and W. An incenter is where two angle bisectors meet, so XZ and YW must pass straight through P: they halve pairs of opposite angles there. The same diagonal point comes from the diagonals AC and BD of the four dots on the circle.

Bradley's circle

The page's claim is that X, Y, Z and W are concyclic. One proof uses the power of a point: with R the external centre of similarity of two of the large incircles, one gets RX · RY = RZ · RW, which puts all four on a circle. The check measures the distance of W from the circle through X, Y and Z on the starting figure, on four fixed figures and on over a thousand generated ones: it never exceeds a few trillionths of a drawing unit. The claim is confirmed for every case tried.

The centre and the extra circles

The centre O′ of Bradley's circle is where the lines A′C′ and B′D′ meet; those join the centres of large incircles of triangles made from the box's corners. The applet draws that point for "Point" and those lines for "Center lines". Its "Second iteration" repeats the whole construction using the tangents to Bradley's circle at X, Y, Z and W; the four new incenters are concyclic as well. The page also claims 1/x + 1/z = 1/y + 1/w for the four small radii, and the check finds that too. One deviation is deliberate: the applet builds its box from tangents at four dots instead of letting you drag the box's corners directly. Every convex tangential quadrilateral can be built this way, so the geometry is the same.

Tick "Small circles" and "Circle", then drag a dot close to its neighbour: the green circle grows, but W stays on it.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
